title: Nobody Can Explain For Sure Why ChatGPT Is So Good At What It Does, Troubling AI Ethics And AI Law
text:
Explain yourself.
That is a somewhat common line that we tend to use when a person has done something that we find questionable or at least perhaps puzzling. Parents are used to asking or shall we say telling their children to explain themselves, especially when a child has gotten into the cookie jar or knocked over an expensive vase.
Explanations are a big deal in life.
I bring up this topic because the role of explanations is increasingly being sought when it comes to the latest in Artificial Intelligence (AI), namely generative AI.
You have undoubtedly heard of or made use of generative AI. OpenAI’s generative AI app ChatGPT and its successor GPT-4 are pretty much part of our societal lexicon these days. ChatGPT is a text-to-text or text-to-essay form of generative AI. You enter a text prompt, and ChatGPT generates or produces a text response, typically consisting of an essay. This is done on an interactive conversational basis using Natural Language Processing (NLP), akin to Siri or Alexa though in writing and generally with much greater fluency.
An ongoing concern for many years has been that we are faced with AI that does a lousy job of explaining how the computational results are being figured out. There is an entire subfield of AI known as XAI (explainable AI) devoted to trying to improve the working features of AI to provide corresponding and apt explanations. I’ve covered XAI extensively in my columns, such as at the link here for example.
Explanations associated with how ChatGPT works and how generative AI overall functions have become a sore spot for critics and those concerned with AI Ethics and AI Law. There is a void associated with this concern. Some AI insiders that recognize the problem are at times suggestive that we should just be happy that it works so well and not be unduly scrutinizing or derogative about the explanatory loosey-goosey underpinnings.
Per a tweet posted on March 20, 2023, by Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT and GPT-4, stated this somewhat droll line: “We offer no explanation as to why [anything works except] divine benevolence.”
I’m betting that you are likely aware that ChatGPT was released in November of last year and has taken the world by storm. People have flocked to using ChatGPT. Headlines proclaim that ChatGPT and generative AI are the hottest types of AI. The hype has been overwhelming at times.
The role of XAI or having an AI app that can explain what it does has been momentarily lost amidst the sea of wonderment associated with generative AI and the popularity of ChatGPT. AI researchers are still working hard on the explainability problem. Meanwhile, the public at large has not especially gotten upset or raised concern that contemporary generative AI tends to not have any capable explanatory functionality per se.
You see, AI researchers and AI makers are hard-pressed to explain how generative AI is as good as it is. I want to make a quick clarification about this. It is usually relatively feasible to proffer a mechanistic explanation, but that’s not the kind of explanation that people usually find particularly useful. A mechanistic explanation is nearly straightforward to derive, though it usually lacks much clarity or insight and ergo is considered an unsatisfactory explanation.
Allow me to elaborate or explain what I mean.
Explaining About Explanations
Suppose that you asked someone to explain how a car works. We’ll make things simplest by focusing on a conventional gasoline-powered automobile also known as an ICE (internal combustion engine).
A child might not have a clue as to how a car works. If you perchance asked a youngster, they might shrug their shoulders and merely say that cars go ahead and can go fast. Not much of an explanation about the inner workings of a vehicle. I’ll label this as a “no explanation” situation. Don’t blame the child, by the way, since answering questions about cars is likely above their pay grade.
An explanation that could be construed as an essence of explanation is the so-called fabricated explanation. We’ll pick on a youngster once again. An exuberant child might gush and tell you that cars work by the efforts of energetic hamsters that are underneath the hood of the vehicle. The hamsters are inside wheels that turn when the enchanting creatures are stoked into running. Those wheels are connected to the tires of the car. Voila, a car gets going once you awaken the hamsters and stir them into running.
What do you think of that explanation?
I’m sure that you laugh at the rather contrived or fabricated explanation. Your understanding of how cars actually work is at odds with this far-fetched hamster explanation. Despite the zany nature of the explanation, you have to admit that it almost seems plausible, at least from the perspective of the child. If the naive toddler has never looked underneath the hood, they might not have any means of disproving the theory that they have concocted. They probably have seen hamsters running on wheels and thus know that the hamster running theorem has some validity. It all adds up, for them.
Not all fabricated explanations are necessarily discardable out of hand.
If you didn’t know anything at all about cars, you might be tempted to believe the fabricated explanation. Unless you have a prior basis for deciding on the authenticity of the explanation, you might have to accept it for the time being. I say this in general and acknowledge that the example of hamsters under the hood is so beyond the pale that you could reject it outright. There are oftentimes fabricated explanations that seem plausible and can readily lead you down a primrose path.
Another type of explanation would be one that is ostensibly on-target but that is shallow or surface oriented. Try this on for size. An adolescent tells you that cars work by the fact that you push down on the gas pedal and the car goes. You have to say that this is generally a correct explanation. Of course, it doesn’t provide much insight. There is nothing said about how the use of the gas pedal magically causes the vehicle to proceed. It is a shallow explanation.
We can turn to another form of explanation, a mechanistic explanation.
A mechanistic explanation provides details and gives you a greater understanding of what is taking place. Here’s how that might go. When you press down on the accelerator pedal, there is a pivot that yanks upon a throttle wire. The throttle wire is in turn connected to a throttle linkage. The throttle linkage accesses a valve that causes air to be allowed into the combustion chamber. An injected mixture of air and gasoline is then sparked to release energy. Etc.
Notice that the mechanistic explanation is essentially a detailed step-by-step indication of what is taking place. Assuming that the mechanistic explanation is accurately depicted, you will have an explanation that somewhat precisely tells you what is happening. That being said, the explanation might seem lacking to you. Yes, it is accurate, but that doesn’t necessarily mean that this has increased your understanding of what is taking place. An analogy might be when schoolchildren are learning arithmetic operations and are sometimes told to mindlessly carry the one and take other actions, they rotely do so even if the detailed explanation of what to do is not at all illuminating to them.
This gets us to the form of explanation that is considered an expressive explanation.
In terms of how a car works, an expressive explanation might be that by pressing on the gas pedal, the gasoline as a fuel enters into a combustion chamber that when sparked will ignite and burn, causing the resultant discharge of energy to push pistons up and down. The piston motion is attached to rods that cause the overall movement to pass through the drivetrain and make the wheels of the car turn. This is more of a how it works explanation that seeks to meld the mechanics with a bit of theory or conceptual background to the matter.
Those are five types of explanations. There are many more. Sometimes an explanation is short and sometimes it is lengthy. Sometimes an explanation is given in one full blast, while on other occasions an explanation is given out in dribbles. Turns out that explaining and how explanations are undertaken is a quite detailed topic, as I have discussed at the link here.
I would also hasten to add that any of the aforementioned five types of explanation has its own time and place.
Imagine that you are in a rush. You have just rented a car. You ask the rental agent how the car works. I dare say you do not want the mechanistic explanation and nor do you likely want the expressive explanation. You already know how cars work overall. In this instance, a shallow explanation is sufficient, such as you need to use the remote key to start the car and then engaging it into gear via the knob on the steering wheel.
There are circumstances too that you do not want an explanation, therefore the “no explanation” option can potentially be perfectly fine. In the case of renting a car, imagine once again that you are in a rush. The rental agent is holding the keys to the car and endlessly explaining all the capabilities of the car and how they work. You just want the keys and urgently seek to get underway with your rental car. No explanation is needed or requested by you.
The gist is that the nature of an explanation can be dependent on its contextual desirability and structure.
Let’s leverage those types of explanations and apply them to generative AI such as ChatGPT.
Here are five essential ways of explaining how generative AI such as ChatGPT works:
- 1) No Explanation. This is the use case wherein no explanation about the generative AI is proffered.
- 2) Fabricated Explanation. This is the use case of a fabricated explanation such as when asking generative AI to explain how it arrived at an answer and you get a contrived or generated response.
- 3) Shallow Explanation. This is an explanation that purports to explain how an answer was derived but is quite shallow and overly surface oriented.
- 4) Mechanistic Explanation. This is an explanation that provides a detailed mechanism-oriented explanation of the step-by-step nature of how a generative AI response was produced.
- 5) Expressive Explanation. This is an explanation that expresses in relatively principled ways how a generative AI response was derived.
We can go ahead and unpack that.
Vital Background About Generative AI
Before I get further into this topic, I’d like to make sure we are all on the same page overall about what generative AI is and also what ChatGPT and GPT-4 are all about. For my ongoing coverage of generative AI and the latest twists and turns, see the link here.
If you are already versed in generative AI such as ChatGPT, you can skim through this foundational portion or possibly even skip ahead to the next section of this discussion. You decide what befits your background and experience.
I’m sure that you already know that ChatGPT is a headline-grabbing AI app that can produce fluent essays and carry on interactive dialogues, almost as though being undertaken by human hands. A person enters a written prompt, ChatGPT responds with a few sentences or an entire essay, and the resulting encounter seems eerily as though another person is chatting with you rather than an AI application. This type of AI is classified as generative AI due to generating or producing its outputs. ChatGPT is a text-to-text generative AI app that takes text as input and produces text as output. I prefer to refer to this as text-to-essay since the outputs are usually of an essay style.
Please know though that this AI and indeed no other AI is currently sentient. Generative AI is based on a complex computational algorithm that has been data trained on text from the Internet and admittedly can do some quite impressive pattern-matching to be able to perform a mathematical mimicry of human wording and natural language. To know more about how ChatGPT works, see my explanation at the link here. If you are interested in the successor to ChatGPT, coined GPT-4, see the discussion at the link here.
There are four primary modes of being able to access or utilize ChatGPT:
- 1) Directly. Direct use of ChatGPT by logging in and using the AI app on the web
- 2) Indirectly. Indirect use of kind-of ChatGPT (actually, GPT-4) as embedded in Microsoft Bing search engine
- 3) App-to-ChatGPT. Use of some other application that connects to ChatGPT via the API (application programming interface)
- 4) ChatGPT-to-App. Now the latest or newest added use entails accessing other applications from within ChatGPT via plugins
The capability of being able to develop your own app and connect it to ChatGPT is quite significant. On top of that capability comes the addition of being able to craft plugins for ChatGPT. The use of plugins means that when people are using ChatGPT, they can potentially invoke your app easily and seamlessly.
I and others are saying that this will give rise to ChatGPT as a platform.
All manner of new apps and existing apps are going to hurriedly connect with ChatGPT. Doing so provides the interactive conversational functionality of ChatGPT. The users of your app will be impressed with the added facility. You will likely get a bevy of new users for your app. Furthermore, if you also provide an approved plugin, this means that anyone using ChatGPT can now make use of your app. This could demonstrably expand your audience of potential users.
As I’ve previously mentioned in my columns, a type of cycle takes place in these circumstances. Sometimes referred to as a network effect, see my analysis at the link here, people tend to join something that others are joining. Facebook was this way. Snapchat was this way. At first, maybe there is little or no traction. But, then, often out of the blue, people start to join. Their friends and colleagues join. Everyone wants to join.
The big get bigger. The small get starved or fail to get any oxygen in the room. That’s the gist of the network effect. It becomes a form of stickiness to the exponential growth factor. People will use what everyone else is using. This in turn makes it more alluring and adds value. The snowball is at times unstoppable and gathers erstwhile momentum.
The temptation to have your app connect with ChatGPT is through the roof. Even if you don’t create an app, you still might be thinking of encouraging your customers or clients to use ChatGPT in conjunction with your everyday services. The problem though is that if they encroach onto banned uses, their own accounts on ChatGPT will also face scrutiny and potentially be locked out by OpenAI.
As noted, generative AI is pre-trained and makes use of a complex mathematical and computational formulation that has been set up by examining patterns in written words and stories across the web. As a result of examining thousands and millions of written passages, the AI can spew out new essays and stories that are a mishmash of what was found. By adding in various probabilistic functionality, the resulting text is pretty much unique in comparison to what has been used in the training set.
There are numerous concerns about generative AI.
One crucial downside is that the essays produced by a generative-based AI app can have various falsehoods embedded, including manifestly untrue facts, facts that are misleadingly portrayed, and apparent facts that are entirely fabricated. Those fabricated aspects are often referred to as a form of AI hallucinations, a catchphrase that I disfavor but lamentedly seems to be gaining popular traction anyway (for my detailed explanation about why this is lousy and unsuitable terminology, see my coverage at the link here).
Another concern is that humans can readily take credit for a generative AI-produced essay, despite not having composed the essay themselves. You might have heard that teachers and schools are quite concerned about the emergence of generative AI apps. Students can potentially use generative AI to write their assigned essays. If a student claims that an essay was written by their own hand, there is little chance of the teacher being able to discern whether it was instead forged by generative AI. For my analysis of this student and teacher confounding facet, see my coverage at the link here and the link here.
There have been some zany outsized claims on social media about Generative AI asserting that this latest version of AI is in fact sentient AI (nope, they are wrong!). Those in AI Ethics and AI Law are notably worried about this burgeoning trend of outstretched claims. You might politely say that some people are overstating what today’s AI can do. They assume that AI has capabilities that we haven’t yet been able to achieve. That’s unfortunate. Worse still, they can allow themselves and others to get into dire situations because of an assumption that the AI will be sentient or human-like in being able to take action.
Do not anthropomorphize AI.
Doing so will get you caught in a sticky and dour reliance trap of expecting the AI to do things it is unable to perform. With that being said, the latest in generative AI is relatively impressive for what it can do. Be aware though that there are significant limitations that you ought to continually keep in mind when using any generative AI app.
One final forewarning for now.
Whatever you see or read in a generative AI response that seems to be conveyed as purely factual (dates, places, people, etc.), make sure to remain skeptical and be willing to double-check what you see.
Yes, dates can be concocted, places can be made up, and elements that we usually expect to be above reproach are all subject to suspicions. Do not believe what you read and keep a skeptical eye when examining any generative AI essays or outputs. If a generative AI app tells you that President Abraham Lincoln flew around the country in a private jet, you would undoubtedly know that this is malarky. Unfortunately, some people might not realize that jets weren’t around in his day, or they might know but fail to notice that the essay makes this brazen and outrageously false claim.
A strong dose of healthy skepticism and a persistent mindset of disbelief will be your best asset when using generative AI.
Into all of this comes a slew of AI Ethics and AI Law considerations.
There are ongoing efforts to imbue Ethical AI principles into the development and fielding of AI apps. A growing contingent of concerned and erstwhile AI ethicists are trying to ensure that efforts to devise and adopt AI takes into account a view of doing AI For Good and averting AI For Bad. Likewise, there are proposed new AI laws that are being bandied around as potential solutions to keep AI endeavors from going amok on human rights and the like. For my ongoing and extensive coverage of AI Ethics and AI Law, see the link here and the link here, just to name a few.
The development and promulgation of Ethical AI precepts are being pursued to hopefully prevent society from falling into a myriad of AI-inducing traps. For my coverage of the UN AI Ethics principles as devised and supported by nearly 200 countries via the efforts of UNESCO, see the link here. In a similar vein, new AI laws are being explored to try and keep AI on an even keel. One of the latest takes consists of a set of proposed AI Bill of Rights that the U.S. White House recently released to identify human rights in an age of AI, see the link here. It takes a village to keep AI and AI developers on a rightful path and deter the purposeful or accidental underhanded efforts that might undercut society.
I’ll be interweaving AI Ethics and AI Law related considerations into this discussion.
Taking Apart The Generative AI Inner Workings
We are ready to further unpack this thorny matter.
I had earlier listed these five core ways of explaining how generative AI such as ChatGPT works:
- 1) No Explanation
- 2) Fabricated Explanation
- 3) Shallow Explanation
- 4) Mechanistic Explanation
- 5) Expressive Explanation
You might not especially care about how ChatGPT or other generative AI work. In that case, the “no explanation” option seems to be your preferred choice.
A fabricated explanation can be generated by simply asking ChatGPT about how it generated or produced a response or answer to your prompt. ChatGPT will provide an essay that seems convincing at first glance. The thing is, the explanation is a fabricated one. It is based on the same pattern-matching capacities as were used when the initial response or answer was generated. You are asking a fabricator to produce an explanation and the result is a fabricated one.
A shallow explanation would be akin to the notion that the generated answer to your prompt was produced via a complex pattern-matching algorithm. This doesn’t tell you much. Imagine that you asked when President Abraham Lincoln was born. Assume that ChatGPT responds that Lincoln was born on February 12, 1809. If you then ask how this answer was derived, being informed that it was based on computational pattern-matching across thousands and millions of pieces of text across the Internet is not an especially helpful explanation. You probably want to know precisely how this answer was derived, such as the specific websites that stated this particular date of birth.
A mechanistic explanation might be more helpful, though it could get you lost in the weeds. Suppose that a tracing of each mathematical calculation and computational pattern-matched element was emitted to showcase how the Lincoln date of birth was supplied as the answer to your prompt. This might consist of many thousands upon thousands of step-by-step calculations and linkages. You probably would scratch your head and find this to be overwhelming.
An expressive explanation would provide a semblance of theory and mechanics to identify how generative AI such as ChatGPT arrives at seemingly human-like responses. At this juncture, the underlying theory is based more on conjecture than proven laws or premises, as I will explain more so next.
Stephen Wolfram provides a fascinating explanation about how generative AI such as ChatGPT is working under the hood in his posted piece entitled “What Is ChatGPT Doing … and Why Does It Work?” dated February 14, 2023.
Consider this key excerpt of his exposition on the matter:
- “What determines this structure? Ultimately it’s presumably some “neural net encoding” of features of human language. But as of now, what those features might be is quite unknown. In effect, we’re “opening up the brain of ChatGPT” (or at least GPT-2) and discovering, yes, it’s complicated in there, and we don’t understand it—even though in the end it’s producing recognizable human language” (ibid).
One quick aside. There are those in AI Ethics that decry the use of references to human biological referents when describing generative AI. The concern is that alluding to generative AI as having a brain or anything along those lines is apt to anthropomorphize AI.
In any case, here are some additional remarks by Wolfram in his essay:
- “But in the end, the remarkable thing is that all these operations—individually as simple as they are—can somehow together manage to do such a good ‘human-like’ job of generating text. It has to be emphasized again that (at least so far as we know) there’s no ‘ultimate theoretical reason’ why anything like this should work. And in fact, as we’ll discuss, I think we have to view this as a—potentially surprising—scientific discovery: that somehow in a neural net like ChatGPT’s it’s possible to capture the essence of what human brains manage to do in generating language” (ibid).
One crucial point is that perhaps our natural languages such as English contain submerged structures that provide a means to readily mimic languages regarding how we compose our sentences and narratives. Perhaps computational and mathematical formulations can land on patterns of natural language in ways that we heretofore had not readily uncovered. The present-day computational statistical analysis at scale and the speed and availability of today’s computing have possibly found vital properties that make the formulation of human-sounding essays and responses a surprisingly “easier” task than otherwise assumed.
Here's how he describes this phenomenon:
- “The specific engineering of ChatGPT has made it quite compelling. But ultimately (at least until it can use outside tools) ChatGPT is ‘merely’ pulling out some ‘coherent thread of text’ from the ‘statistics of conventional wisdom’ that it’s accumulated. But it’s amazing how human-like the results are. And as I’ve discussed, this suggests something that’s at least scientifically very important: that human language (and the patterns of thinking behind it) are somehow simpler and more ‘law like’ in their structure than we thought. ChatGPT has implicitly discovered it. But we can potentially explicitly expose it, with semantic grammar, computational language, etc. (ibid).
Recall that at the start of this discussion, I mentioned that explanations are an important part of our lives.
Let’s shift this into the legal realm.
There are many ways in which an explanation makes or breaks a legal case or legal matter. Explanations are not merely of a whim or happenstance. They are at times a requirement and must meet legal scrutiny.
A recent talk by FTC Commissioner Alvaro Bedoya entitled “Early Thoughts on Generative AI” that was posted online proffered these insights about the fact that generative AI currently relies upon unexplained unarticulated facets:
- “I want to note that the law sometimes demands explanation – and that the inexplicability or unpredictability of a product is rarely a legally cognizable defense.”
- “ What do I mean by that?”
- “Looking solely on laws that the FTC enforces, both the Fair Credit Reporting Act and the Equal Credit Opportunity Act requires explanations for certain kinds of adverse decisions. Under our section 5 authority, we have frequently brought actions against companies for the failure to take reasonable measures to prevent reasonably foreseeable risks. And the Commission has historically not responded well to the idea that a company is not responsible for their product because that product is a ‘black box’ that was unintelligible or difficult to test.”
- “I urge companies who are creating or using AI products for important eligibility decisions to closely consider that the ability to explain your product and predict the risks that it will generate may be critical to your ability to comply with the law” (source: online posting “Prepared Remarks of Commissioner Alvaro M. Bedoya, Federal Trade Commission”, “Before the International Association of Privacy Professionals”, April 5, 2023).
Any AI maker that simply shrugs their shoulders about the AI explainability aspects of generative AI would be wise to consult their legal counsel.
Inevitably, legal confrontations about these matters are going to arise. Of course, AI makers should already be seeking the advice of their legal counsel about the Intellectual Property (IP) infringement and plagiarism allegations that are already being voiced about generative AI and will inexorably grow louder and louder, see my coverage at the link here. Only a few such lawsuits are underway now. The expectation is that if some of those prevail, the floodgates will be opened and AI makers will have their hands full with trying to stay above water.
Conclusion
Sometimes explanations are fully needed.
AI makers are put on notice that they are veering into murky territory by not being able to sufficiently explain how their generative AI works. Of course, they can resort to showcasing a detailed mechanistic tracing, though whether this passes muster as a sufficient and suitable form of explanation will need to be decided by our courts.
There is another angle to this conundrum about AI and explanations that you might either find completely serious and crucial or that you might disregard out of hand and view as fanciful.
Here it is.
If we are on our way toward Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), which is the kind of AI that would exhibit human intelligence and perhaps be considered sentient AI, the concern is that we ought to know for sure what is going on inside of these budding AI systems. Generative AI ought to be as cut and dried and open as can be. This might help us to stave off the existential risks that are being bandied around, such as that AGI might decide to enslave humankind or possibly wipe us out entirely, see my discussion of these risks at the link here.
Allowing the latest in AI to exist as a kind of impenetrable black box has got the hairs raising on the necks of those in AI Ethics and AI Law that we are possibly going to proceed into unknown waters. One thing after another might start to add up in the most endangered of ways. Meanwhile, without having been able to probe and ascertain how AI has risen to levels of human-like talents, we are walking possibly into a deadly trap of our own making.
Heavy stuff.
I’ll try to make some final remarks for now that are a bit lighter in tone.
An explanation can at times ruin the mystery and fun of a matter at hand. When you go to see a magic act, the excitement, and awe come from not getting a full-on explanation of how the trick worked. The same can be said about trying to explain a joke. The famous author Mark Twain said this about such circumstances: “Explaining humor is a lot like dissecting a frog, you learn a lot in the process, but in the end you kill it.”
Noted playwright Eugene Ionesco provided this piece of wisdom about the role of explanations: “Explanation separates us from astonishment, which is the only gateway to the incomprehensible.”
Are we satisfied with generative AI to the degree that we aren’t clamoring for underlying expressive explanations or are we potentially laying the groundwork for some existential risk by not making sure that we know precisely how the magic is being made? A cynic might suggest that if we don’t nail down the inner workings of generative AI such as ChatGPT, we might be on a formidable and leery path toward Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) that is altogether incomprehensible to us. Others might exhort that there is no need to dig into the magic and we ought to relish the results either way.
Whatever posture you take on this, please make sure to explain, one way or another, the nature of your position, doing so expressively.

title: Council Post: Generative AI For B2B Marketing: Use Cases And Challenges
text:
By Anna Anisin, founder at DataScience.Salon, overseeing community and business development.
Marketing is one of the fields that I believe can significantly benefit from the power of AI tools like ChatGPT.
ChatGPT has been widely discussed among the Data Science Salon community, and that’s why I wanted you to know what it means to the field of marketing. AI has already provided many marketers with great results through solutions such as recommender systems or customer service chatbots, and tools like ChatGPT could provide even bigger opportunities for the field. This post will discuss how companies can leverage large language models (LLMs) and generative AI for marketing and what they should keep in mind when doing so.
Marketing Use Cases
Chatbots For Customer Support
Traditional chatbots give automated responses, often without a complete understanding of a user's intent. This can make some of the answers irrelevant even when they're accurate.
With generative AI and LLMs, you can build engaging AI assistants that can comprehend the context around users' queries and follow up on their responses to provide human-like guidance.
The assistants could also recommend relevant products or services to help customers find what they're searching for more quickly.
Content Generation
Whether it's for product descriptions, blog posts, long-form articles, advertisements, sales copy or emails, LLMs like ChatGPT can generate every type of content using a given prompt.
They also have the potential to rewrite or paraphrase existing content in different tones and styles to have a wider reach without additional cost or time.
Additionally, organizations can use this tool to generate inspirational ideas: for example, by asking what type of ad design would attract a particular industry group.
New Hire Training
Selling to businesses is often more complex than dealing with B2C customers, as companies may require more informative advertisements than persuasive ones.
As such, the marketing staff must be well-trained to handle complex business queries concerning long-term contractual agreements, bulk purchases, customer-specific pricing and so on.
LLMs can quickly give marketers relevant insights to help them understand what issues business customers face and improve product or service offerings accordingly.
Market Research
AI can help marketers understand how a specific customer segment behaves and generate marketing briefs for quick execution.
Organizations can plan effective marketing strategies using such information without conducting expensive surveys or focus groups.
Challenges Of Using AI Models For Marketing
Content Originality
While LLMs can generate engaging content, there's a question about their originality. Since these models generally train on existing content that's available on the internet, it is challenging to identify ownership and accuracy.
The user should always fact-check and proofread AI-generated content before publishing it online. The slightest error can undermine their reputation in the business realm.
Also keep in mind that you have to be very careful when actually using AI-generated content on your website because Google discourages poor-quality or problematic AI content.
Prompt Accuracy
The output of any generative AI model is as good as the prompt a user provides. A misleading prompt could produce inaccurate results and may also provide biased information.
Giving concise, simple and clear prompts is always better, and it's important to avoid ambiguities. But learning to do so is time-consuming.
Generative AI And B2B Marketing In The Future
AI is undoubtedly transforming the way marketers create content and engage with their target audiences.
I believe tools like ChatGPT will soon become mainstream marketing tools, which could open doors for a paradigm shift. However, marketers should be aware of the tools’ limitations and use them with caution to avoid unethical practices such as content plagiarism, bias and manipulative marketing.

title: Analysis | The Taxman Will Eventually Come for AI, Too
text:
There are a lot of dramatic and profound questions about AI, but some of the most important ones are mundane. For instance: Should AI agents, when they perform productive work, be required to pay taxes?
One option is to let AI bots work tax-free, like honeybees do. At first that might make life simple for the IRS, but a problem of tax arbitrage will arise. Tax-free AI labor would have a pronounced competitive advantage over its taxed human counterpart. Furthermore, too many AIs will be released into the commons. Why own an AI and pay taxes when you can program it to do your bidding, renounce ownership, and enjoy its services tax-free? It seems easy enough to disclaim ownership of autonomous bots, especially if they are producing autonomous bots of their own. If nothing else, you could sell them to shell corporations.
The obvious alternative is to tax AI labor. Laboring AIs would have to file tax returns, which they may be capable of doing in the very near future. (Can they claim deductions for their baby AIs? What about their investments?)
Since AIs do not enjoy leisure as humans do, arguably their labor should be taxed at a higher rate than that of humans. Still, AIs shouldn’t be taxed too much. At prohibitively high rates of taxation, AIs will have lower stocks of wealth to invest in improving themselves, which in turn would lower long-run tax revenue from AI labor. Yes, they’re AIs, but incentives still matter.
Some people might fear that super-patient, super-smart AIs will accumulate too much wealth, though either investments or labor, and thereby hold too much social influence. That would create a case for a wealth tax on AIs, in addition to an income tax. But if AIs are such good investors, humans will also want the social benefits that accrue from such wisdom, and that again implies rates of taxation well below the confiscatory level.
Additionally, maybe there should be a kind of gift tax, paid by humans, on any benefits we receive from an AI, whether we own it or not. But discovering and estimating the value of those gifts seems beyond the capacities of the current IRS, even if augmented by some AI assistants.
The fundamental problem here is that AIs might be very good at providing in-kind services — improving organizational software, responding to emails, and so on. It is already a problem for the tax system when neighbors barter services, but the AIs will take this kind of relationship to a much larger scale.
Forget about hiring AIs, actually: What if you invest in them, tell them to do your bidding, repudiate your ownership, and then let them run much of your business and life? You could write off your investment in the AI as a business expense, and subsequently receive tax-free in-kind services, in what would amount to a de facto act of exchange.
A major topic in AI circles is “alignment,” namely whether humans can count on AI agents to do our bidding, rather than mounting destructive cyberattacks or destroying us. These investments in alignment are necessary and important. But the more successful humans become at alignment, the larger the problem with tax arbitrage.
It is not obvious how the tax system ought to respond to these more complex possibilities. Granted, in the short run, these problems are likely small. But progress in AI services has been extremely rapid as of late, and that trend may well continue.
A deeper analysis would consider AIs that developed proclivities to work much less if they were taxed at too high a rate. That in turn would lower the optimal tax rate on AIs. What about an AI that refused to work at all, at any positive tax rate? What if Estonia or El Salvador promised to let their AIs work for you tax-free, or at rates of 5%? Would the humans or the AIs win those battles of will and attrition?
If GPT-4 doesn’t already have this figured out, GPT-5 might. Or better yet, a specialized AI tax-policy bot can be created to figure it out. Just don’t forget to ask for a W-9.

title: Council Post: How To Make Generative AI The Robin To Your Batman
text:
Eric Vermillion is the CEO of Helpshift.
Ever since its launch in November 2022, OpenAI’s ChatGPT has quickly become one of the most buzzworthy and disruptive new technologies of the past decade. People in all kinds of professions are experimenting with new ways to research, write code and create content with the power of generative AI.
However, some critics and skeptics have raised doubts about ChatGPT, worrying that the technology delivers too many inaccurate results, thus forcing people to spend too much time fact-checking and correcting the AI’s output. Major Wall Street banks are limiting or prohibiting the use of ChatGPT (paywall) by their employees, with concerns around the accuracy of information and possible regulatory issues.
Companies need to know the risks and limitations before going “all in” on generative AI. But as the CEO of a company that offers tools like chatbots and helpbot automation software, I believe this new technology is nothing to fear. Instead, it’s an opportunity for all of us as a society to think about how we can interact with AI and harness these tools to do more of what people do best. For business leaders, software developers, marketers, content creators, customer support teams and other professionals, generative AI can be a helpful sidekick: the “Robin” to your “Batman.”
Will Generative AI Eliminate Your Job? Probably Not …
The prospect of human workers being replaced by automation has always been a source of anxiety, ever since the rise of the steam engine and the Industrial Revolution. But today, even knowledge workers and creative professionals who never thought software could do their jobs are starting to feel unsettled by the speed and versatility of generative AI. Will it make human creativity obsolete?
The short answer is “no!” You’re unlikely to be replaced by AI, but you might be replaced by another person who uses AI more effectively than you can. Generative AI is a new tool, and as with any knowledge work tool, the people who can utilize it effectively are going to be at an advantage. It might not be the right fit for every company or role, but you can’t just wish it away. Instead of being afraid of generative AI, people should learn how to use it to their best advantage.
As the technology gets smarter, here are a few examples of how people might soon be able to use generative AI tools at work:
• Get quick answers when conducting research.
• Brainstorm different ways to present their next marketing campaign.
• Help customer service teams with their tone and the way they respond, ensuring a more personalized and professional response.
• Use it as an “auto-complete” tool to generate prompts and paragraphs for business communication—so it anticipates what you need to say, and gives you the chance to enhance, edit and personalize the message.
• Help developers write code (or debug code) more quickly.
We’re not at the point where AI in itself is going to replace humans, especially not for higher-value, more complex, context-rich creative work. But I think generative AI is going to significantly improve human performance. Don’t think of this as a battle of “humans versus AI;” instead, embrace the opportunities of “humans plus AI.”
Using ChatGPT For Enhanced Customer Service
AI-powered chatbots have become more common in customer service in the past few years, but sometimes customers get frustrated with the limitations of chatbots that don’t understand the context of what people are asking or that offer a limited range of response options. The most powerful chatbots are ones that are programmed to help with routine, repetitive customer service queries like frequently asked questions or troubleshooting common problems like how to reset a password.
Generative AI has the potential to provide higher-level responses to customers—but don’t let the AI go it alone. It would be a mistake to assume that it can just “replace” your customer service team or create all your customer service content.
Instead, use it to work alongside your human team. Tools like ChatGPT can help create an FAQ article in minutes that used to take a human 1–2 hours. Your customer support people should fill in the gaps, add product-specific details and edit the output of the tool.
Generative AI can also assist agents by recommending responses for low-complexity queries. It should free up your customer care team to spend more time and attention on higher-value, complex problems that require human insight.
Overcoming The Uncanny Valley Of AI
Generative AI tools like ChatGPT represent a huge leap forward in the capabilities of AI. However, brands still need to recognize the limitations and proceed with appropriate caution and practicality. The biggest risk I see of generative AI for brands is that some companies will move too fast and try to let the tools do too many tasks on their own. We still need people to interact with these tools and guide their work in the right direction, especially for roles like customer support.
The output of generative AI tools sometimes sounds like an “uncanny valley” version of human language—the syntax is correct and the words sound right, but the actual content or important details might be wrong. You might need to re-read and edit the output to make sure it’s sending the correct message for your brand with precise accuracy.
For customer support, generative AI can be a risk if it’s not receiving good oversight from your human team. Left unedited, the AI might give your customer bad instructions or incomplete steps. For example, it might tell your customer, “To change your payment method, complete these three steps,” even though the process requires five steps. Different brands have different levels of risk tolerance and complexity needs for their customer support responses. If you’re trying to give support for a $10,000 problem, AI might be too risky.
Alternatively, if you can manage the risks and limitations, leaving this technology on the sidelines could be missing an opportunity to leverage powerful capabilities to help agents resolve issues quickly.
At the end of the day, it should be a productivity sidekick and an extension of the human mind. However, we still need people who can harness these tools to do more of what people do best.

title: Council Post: AI Demystified: Making Sense Of Artificial Intelligence For Your Business
text:
Nicholas Domnisch is the CEO & Partner of EES Health, an NYC-based software development agency empowering innovation in digital health.
Since the release of ChatGPT, talk of artificial intelligence has taken over, and rightfully so. It presents a leap forward in our ability to automate processes and optimize cost efficiency. In the midst of a hype cycle, however, it is good to remain cautious. Do you remember when everyone got sucked into the NFT craze? Those investments haven’t always panned out. Recently, Meta stopped support for digital collectibles on Instagram and Facebook after investing heavily.
All of this is not to say that AI is bad, but rather to offer a word of advice. Approach the topic with thoughtful intent. In this article, I will outline the three different stages of AI and how to look at them. For relevance, we will zoom in on a specific industry: healthcare. Healthcare is traditionally a technology laggard, but at the same time, there are countless opportunities to innovate.
Let’s break AI down into two buckets: narrow AI and general AI. Narrow AI is the AI we have today. It is good at automating manual, repetitive and structured tasks. But it isn’t creative or knowledgeable outside of its narrow focus. General AI, on the other hand, can learn about and do pretty much anything. Note we do not have functional general AI today.
Why is this important? Because you need to know, specifically, how AI can help your business. You need to know what should be built in-house, what should be outsourced and what belongs in the R&D pipeline.
In-House Development
If you want an AI implementation now, turn your attention to narrow AI. Think about tasks that are manual, repetitive and structured. For example, in healthcare, clinical efficiency can be improved, especially in areas like administration and revenue cycle management. I will explain below.
Administrative Tasks: Is your office constantly inundated with administrative work? Companies such as OnShift and Cedar are utilizing AI to optimize scheduling appointments, managing patient records and billing, which is freeing up healthcare professionals to focus on patient care.
Information Verification: Electronic health records services like Athena and Health Gorilla are using AI to automatically match and verify patient information and insurance eligibility. This will eliminate hours of work manually checking patient insurance information by calling insurance providers or previous physicians.
Virtual Assistants: AI-powered virtual assistants and chatbots, like ChatGPT or Google LaMDA, can provide patients with 24/7 support, answering questions and providing personalized care management advice.
Technology Partnership Opportunities
Various third-party AI providers have spent years developing complex and creative AI solutions. For you to mimic their development would require specialized expertise and a significant development lift. Instead, you should look to partner with those who have already done the groundwork. Below, I will outline some potential partnership opportunities for healthcare organizations to level up their AI usage.
Medical Imaging: AI can help in the analysis and interpretation of medical images such as x-rays, MRIs and CT scans. For example, Philips and Aidoc are empowering radiologists to identify irregularities that went previously unseen.
Clinical Decision Support: By integrating voice recognition and sensor technology into hospital environments, providers can streamline their workflows and focus on patient care. In healthcare, companies like care.ai and Nvidia partnered to create AI systems that help healthcare providers make informed patient decisions.
Care Coordination: AI can help patients navigate their care journey by providing real-time recommendations and alerts based on personal health data. As an example, AI care coordination systems, like viz.ai and Dina, can provide real-time decision support, suggesting treatment options based on the patient's medical history and current symptoms.
Looking Into The Future
At this point, we have exhausted the utility of narrow AI, and it is time to evaluate R&D opportunities. As AI improves, its utility will expand exponentially. Do you know where you want to position yourself going forward? General AI doesn’t exist today, but it will.
In healthcare, technology adoption has been slow. Medical robots are used in surgeries. But the burden of clinical decision-making still lies largely on the shoulders of doctors. In the future, can AI lift some of that burden away and improve overall clinical efficacy?
Disease Detection: Clinics can use AI to find patterns that were previously undetectable. For perspective, Freenome and ArtiQ are analyzing patients' biomarker data to improve early cancer and lung disease detection.
Medical Research: By expanding medical data collection to more providers and additional AI simulations, Topography Health and Unlearn are accelerating the pace of medical research and helping to develop new treatments and therapies.
Surgical Planning: AI can analyze large datasets to identify patterns and predict potential complications before they occur, enabling personalized care. MindTrace and Theator use AI to help surgeons plan and execute surgeries for each specific patient.
Final Word Of Caution
AI implementation is not risk-free. Before doing anything, evaluate each risk specific to your situation. Below, I will outline a few key AI technology risks in the healthcare industry.
Cost Of Integration: The integration of AI systems with existing or complex healthcare infrastructure will require a significant investment in development and training resources.
Training Bias: AI algorithms can learn and reinforce any biases that already exist in training data. This can lead to inaccurate or discriminatory health outcomes.
Limited Transparency: AI systems often operate as "black boxes," meaning that the underlying algorithms and decision-making processes are not transparent, which can lead to mistrust and a lack of accountability.
Looking at history, we can see that the benefits of innovation have outweighed the associated risks. Being the disruptor puts you in the driver's seat. Being an industry leader in data privacy, consumer protection and AI ethics can only be achieved by those who seek to move first.
Companies on the sidelines will be forced to follow in the footsteps of those before them. So, if you seek to be an innovator, charge ahead. But do so with structure. Move methodically from low-level automation, complex narrow AI implementation and, only then, onto general AI R&D.

title: Council Post: Is Your Leadership Working Together To Navigate AI?
text:
CEO of Making Science with over 25 years of experience in tech. We are a 360º digital acceleration partner.
Everywhere you look, media and industry pros are discussing artificial intelligence (AI). With ChatGPT featured on every news site and its technology pushing Bing to make a big comeback, as well as Bard emerging as its Google competitor, enterprises are putting skin in the game announcing increased investments in AI technology. As these new technologies and applications are ushered in, new challenges follow.
In essence, we're collectively navigating these advancements and associated challenges. But, at the core, leadership within organizations is ultimately responsible for paving the path to adoption. Therefore, leadership must take the reigns and drive AI adoption and implementation cross-functionally to determine how organizations can work within an evolving technology framework and embrace this emerging tech while creating alignment across the board.
Let’s lay the groundwork—namely, the size and significance of the more recent applications of AI, such as ChatGPT. ChatGPT is a streamlined version of AI technology—a chatbot-like function that answers prompts submitted by a user. It’s like using a search engine to find what you need, but the results are more intelligent and focused on answering the prompt.
With its simplistic user interface, the platform set a record for the fastest user growth by hitting 100 million active users in January 2023, only two months after its launch. In comparison, TikTok reached 100 million users nine months after launch, and Instagram took 2.5 years to acquire the same. In addition to its simplicity, this quick adoption is attributed to the breadth of the application and curiosity fueled by virality.
Regardless of the popularity and accelerated adoption, a tool that can streamline processes and make work simpler or more efficient is just the cusp of what AI can do and how it can impact our daily lives. This is precisely why organizations must align their approach and start at the top—with leadership.
Bring Leadership Together
Great leaders recognize that their teams have vastly different experiences and knowledge bases. Therefore, some may be more excited than others about AI. Some leaders may be unaware of the challenges—or benefits—and be reluctant to deploy a new technology amid so many unknowns.
For example, a CTO may be researching the security implications of the technology and concerned about breaches, data storage and internal misuse. Meanwhile, the CMO might be aware of use cases that enable systems integrations that merge datasets with creative assets and speed up production, which can accelerate new product launches and go-to-market initiatives.
The dichotomy of benefits versus risk requires an open conversation in which everyone has a seat at the table and equal time to voice their opinions and ask questions. More on that to come.
Highlighting The Benefits
Let’s back up for a moment to understand why this conversation must be had in the first place. Aside from the increasing popularity of AI platforms and the undeniable fact that new tools will be built to improve business functions, most view AI as a game-changer. This technology is a way to automate and augment existing functions that previously required a human touch because it was the only option.
A few key potential benefits of AI include:
- Creating efficiencies in communication and general workflows.
- Providing personalization throughout the digital customer experience.
- Supporting content generation and campaign ideas.
- Accelerating the ideation process.
Although the potential benefits are pretty clear, AI does require a certain skill set and talent to achieve the desired results (and new AI-based jobs are emerging in high demand). But it’s not as simple as, “Let’s use ChatGPT and our marketing will be twice as fast, and we'll grow exponentially.” Implementation and integration require a solid understanding, guardrails for use and leadership that actively wants to embrace it.
Bringing It All Together
Leaders should embrace this change—and the sooner, the better. Here are some ways to bring leadership together before you miss out on riding this wave.
Share knowledge.
As mentioned, not every leader will join the table coming from the same knowledge base and perspective. Instead of making assumptions about who knows what, level the playing field and share foundational knowledge. Provide use cases that show both the benefits and challenges, and invite open conversations for leaders to ask questions, challenge ideals and learn from each other. Consider posing it as a hypothesis to your team: "If we embrace AI now, what could some of the outcomes be?" This will likely be a recurring conversation, so set the expectation that this open dialogue is not “one and done.” Instead, allow it to be an open forum and an ongoing, evolving conversation.
Keep concerns top of mind.
During the leadership meeting, be sure to give everyone adequate time to share their concerns and how they relate to business objectives. For example, there may be concerns about talent, time and tools. Departments may be wondering how they'll find or train the right people to implement the technology, especially because much is in its infancy. If this is a concern, work together to identify outside resources such as agencies, technology partners or temporary staff that can assist. Bottomline: Give everyone the time and space to share and show that these concerns will be addressed now and in the future.
Provide resources.
To keep everyone informed and aware of the changes or tools to assist with adoption, use and management, provide a place where leaders can share and access tools. Offer articles, reputable influencers and other professional development options that will support leaders without requiring them to find information on their own.
The speed at which AI is accelerating in the current environment is jarring, but the last few years taught us something valuable: The unexpected can be managed successfully. Keeping an open mind and setting the tone for AI adoption at the top will create a more agile environment and a flexible group of leaders who'll understand that technology is an enabler, but it will only be as powerful as the team behind it.

title: Three Important Measures To Ensure Ethical Practices In A World Of Emerging AI
text:
Sadly, the world of AI has moved from ethics washing to ethics squashing.
Microsoft recently laid off its entire ethics and society team. The team was responsible for transforming the principles created by Microsoft’s Office of Responsible AI into consistent rules and practices. It was also tasked with anticipating the risks that AI could pose to people and society, and most recently, it had been evaluating Microsoft’s adoption of OpenAI’s technology. It’s no secret that Microsoft has made massive bets on OpenAI, investing $11 billion in the startup and infusing ChatGPT’s capabilities into Bing and across its suite of products. A team whose very function was to pump the brakes was bound to get run over.
This is just the most recent example of AI ethics falling by the wayside. In 2020, Timnit Gebru, a researcher focused on the ethics of AI at Google, was infamously terminated after publishing a paper highlighting the danger of biases in large language models. Google executives took exception to a paper she coauthored that criticized a technology with massive commercial potential.
Unfortunately, tech companies haven’t learned that prioritizing profitability over principles is short-sighted and that the long-term impact can hurt your brand and society at large.
Shape Your Own Ethical Destiny — Don’t Let Tech Providers Do It For You
It’s not just technology companies that are grappling with these ethical dilemmas. Banks using AI to make credit decisions and detect fraud, healthcare companies using AI for medical diagnoses, and governments using AI to provide essential services all need to navigate these ethical waters. Unfortunately, the “leaders” in AI are setting a poor example. Relying on them to build AI ethically will expose you to reputational and regulatory risk. Here are some ways to mitigate these risks:
- Third-party due diligence. Companies adopting solutions from Microsoft, Google, and other AI technology providers will ultimately be held accountable both legally and in the court of public opinion for any ethical missteps. Effective third-party due diligence will therefore be essential and will require tight coordination between your procurement, risk and compliance, and data science teams. Demand explainability from vendors — don’t trust vendors that refuse to grant transparency into how their systems work.
- Fairness assessments. AI inherits the biases within its training data. As large language models are in their infancy, the biases within them are still being discovered. Without dedicated teams at vendors to perform this research, these biases are likely to manifest in commercialized products that you use to interact with customers and run your business. Companies should start measuring a variety of fairness metrics to prevent discriminatory outcomes.
- Enterprisewide AI governance. Enterprises should build their AI governance programs across four pillars — purpose, action, culture, and assessment — to ensure compliance with internal policies and with coming regulations such as the EU’s AI Act and New York City’s Local Law 144. Be on the lookout for Forrester’s AI governance report in the next month or so.
We’re in the midst of an AI renaissance. Emerging AI technologies such as large language models will shape the future of business and quite possibly the future of our species. We need ethical gatekeepers to ensure that this future is the one we want to live in. Surely, it’s worth the cost.

Waiting for quantum computers to arrive, software engineers get creative
Once too big for conventional computers, these algorithms are finally being put to work thanks to today's powerful artificial intelligence chips, industry executives told Reuters.
By Jane Lanhee Lee
OAKLAND, California: Quantum computers promise to be millions of times faster than today's fastest supercomputers, potentially revolutionizing everything from medical research to the way people solve problems of climate change. The wait for these machines, though, has been long, despite the billions poured into them.
But the uncertainty and the dismal stock performance of publicly-listed quantum computer companies including Rigetti Computing Inc have not scared investors away. Some are turning to startups who are pivoting to using powerful chips to run quantum-inspired software on regular computers as they bide their time.
Lacking quantum computers that customers can use today to get an advantage over classical computers, these startups are developing a new breed of software inspired by algorithms used in quantum physics, a branch of science that studies the fundamental building blocks of nature.
Once too big for conventional computers, these algorithms are finally being put to work thanks to today's powerful artificial intelligence chips, industry executives told Reuters.
QC Ware, a software startup that has raised more than $33 million and initially focused only on software that could run on quantum computers, said it needed to change tack and find a solution for clients today until the future quantum machines arrive.
So QC Ware CEO Matt Johnson said it turned to Nvidia Corp's graphic processing units (GPU) to "figure out how can we get them something that is a big step change in performance ... and build a bridge to quantum processing in the future."
GPUs are microchips that were made to process video for gaming and became so powerful that they do the bulk of AI computing today. They are now being used in quantum development, as well.
This week, QC Ware is unveiling a quantum-inspired software platform called Promethium that will simulate chemical molecules - to see how they interact with things like protein - on a traditional computer using GPUs.
The software can cut simulation time from hours to minutes for molecules of 100 atoms, and months to hours for molecules of up to 2000 atoms, compared with existing software solutions, said QC Ware's head of quantum chemistry Robert Parrish.
$1 BILLION RAISED
Big-name investors and funds are backing the future, such as Alphabet Inc's former chairman Eric Schmidt, asset manager T. Rowe Price, Samsung Ventures, and the venture arm of U.S. intelligence agencies In-Q-Tel.

OAKLAND, California: Quantum computers promise to be millions of times faster than today's fastest supercomputers, potentially revolutionizing everything from medical research to the way people solve problems of climate change. The wait for these machines, though, has been long, despite the billions poured into them.
But the uncertainty and the dismal stock performance of publicly-listed quantum computer companies including Rigetti Computing Inc have not scared investors away. Some are turning to startups who are pivoting to using powerful chips to run quantum-inspired software on regular computers as they bide their time.
Lacking quantum computers that customers can use today to get an advantage over classical computers, these startups are developing a new breed of software inspired by algorithms used in quantum physics, a branch of science that studies the fundamental building blocks of nature.
Once too big for conventional computers, these algorithms are finally being put to work thanks to today's powerful artificial intelligence chips, industry executives told Reuters.
QC Ware, a software startup that has raised more than $33 million and initially focused only on software that could run on quantum computers, said it needed to change tack and find a solution for clients today until the future quantum machines arrive.
So QC Ware CEO Matt Johnson said it turned to Nvidia Corp's graphic processing units (GPU) to "figure out how can we get them something that is a big step change in performance ... and build a bridge to quantum processing in the future."
GPUs are microchips that were made to process video for gaming and became so powerful that they do the bulk of AI computing today. They are now being used in quantum development, as well.
This week, QC Ware is unveiling a quantum-inspired software platform called Promethium that will simulate chemical molecules - to see how they interact with things like protein - on a traditional computer using GPUs.
The software can cut simulation time from hours to minutes for molecules of 100 atoms, and months to hours for molecules of up to 2000 atoms, compared with existing software solutions, said QC Ware's head of quantum chemistry Robert Parrish.
